title: Training with a coach who speaks another language
summary: How shooters, coaches and organisers prepare a session with a coach from another country, with an interpreter or without one, and what changes at a competition.

body.html: Many shooters train with a coach from another country, at home or on a trip. It works well when everyone prepares a little: the coach, the shooter and, if there is one, the interpreter. Many misunderstandings come from words that nobody agreed on beforehand.
Safety comes first. Make sure each shooter has understood the safety briefing before anyone loads. If anyone is unsure, have it interpreted or shown again.

html: Before the session, agree on the key terms: the coach’s words for lead and misses, and for the pick-up point, hold point and break point.
Agree on the coach’s hand signals and on a pause sign, such as a raised palm.
The coach speaks in short phrases and waits for the translation.
Talk only when the gun is open, not during the shooter’s routine.
After an explanation, check understanding: ask the shooter to show it, not just to say “yes”.

body.html: Short cues on the stand are often whispered from behind (chuchotage). Briefings and debriefs work better when the coach says a sentence or two, pauses, and the interpreter translates (consecutive interpreting). More for interpreters: Where to stand and when to speak.

At a competition the rules change everything. In both disciplines, coaching during the competition is forbidden: the shooter gets a yellow card, and the coach is sent out of the shooting area (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition). The rules do not mention interpreters, so passing on advice could be treated as coaching. The interpreter passes on only official information from the referee, the jury and the organiser. Plan all coaching for training days and debriefs.

Without an interpreter, a small shared vocabulary goes a long way. About twenty anchor words cover much of a session; you will find them in the phrases below. Learn them before the first lesson, in the coach’s language.

Show rather than tell. Ask the coach to trace the line with his hand, to point to the pick-up point and the break point, or to demonstrate the mount. Short videos of your shots help both of you to see the same thing.

After the session, write down the two or three main points in both languages, or ask the coach to send them. A one-page bilingual sheet with the anchor words, the coach’s signals and the referee’s calls helps on the next day too.

For organisers of training trips: send the coach and the group the bilingual sheet before the trip. Plan an interpreter at least for the safety briefing, even if the rest of the session runs without one.

key_points.html: Agree on words, hand signals and a pause sign before the session
Talk only when the gun is open
Check understanding: ask the shooter to show, not just to say yes
At a competition: no coaching; the interpreter passes on only official information
Without an interpreter: about twenty anchor words, show instead of tell, notes in both languages

quiz.q: A coach and a shooter share no language. What helps most in the first session?

options.text: Agreed anchor words and hand signals
A translation app during the routine

quiz.explain: A small agreed vocabulary and the coach’s signals carry most of a session; long explanations and phones during the routine get in the way.

quiz.q: At a competition, the shooter’s coach asks the interpreter to pass on a tip. What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly between targets
Pass it on with the referee’s nod
Pass it on only between stands
Decline: pass on only official words

quiz.explain: Coaching during the competition is forbidden, and the rules do not mention interpreters. Passing on only the referee, the jury and the organiser protects the shooter.

quiz.q: When should the coach and the interpreter talk to the shooter on the stand?
quiz.explain: The shooter’s routine ends with the shot, and by the time the gun is closed it is well under way; words during it break the shooter’s focus.
